title: Every Harness Will Become A Claw — Sam Bhagwat, Mastra

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk's primary focus is agent harness architecture, including agent loops, planning, parallel subagents, skills, and the evolution from harnesses to claws. The talk discusses agent architecture concepts broadly applicable across domains, presented to developers building agent systems. The talk draws on 18 months of agents in production and discusses the production evolution of harnesses into claws. The talk assumes familiarity with agents, LLMs, and context engineering while remaining conceptual rather than deeply technical. This is a conference presentation delivered at the AI Engineer channel. Six direct transcript quotes support the classification across all key themes of harness architecture and evolution.

summary: Sam Bhagwat, co-founder and CEO of Mastra (a TypeScript agent framework) and author of 'Principles of Building AI Agents,' frames the talk around an ascending agentic spectrum: LLMs, agents, harnesses, and claws. An agent differs from an LLM by adding the agent loop, tool calls, memory, retry of failed tasks, context engineering, and agent state. Harnesses add further qualities: durability and doggedness (running for hours or days, resuming interrupted streams), planning mode, parallel subagents, TUI and slash commands, skills, dynamic agent creation, background bash tasks, autocompact when context fills, thread persistence, queue/steer/interrupt capability, and session-long tool approval. Sam observes a recent shift from local harnesses to always-on cloud harnesses—agents accessible via Slack (including multi-user), mobile apps, cloud sandboxes enabling greater parallelism, and PRs pushed directly to GitHub. The harness-to-claw transition adds initiative and learning: agents listen to external feeds, have a heartbeat that wakes them periodically, offer channels like text/WhatsApp/Telegram, store memory accessibly, run as daemons with gateways, perform continual learning via automatic skill generation or code modification. He coins Steinberger's law (a spinoff of Zawinski's law): every harness will expand until it becomes a claw, driven by technological, economic, and psychological forces. To survive the predicted shakeout, a claw must be either economically valuable or frequently used—otherwise it is forgotten, like a college friend who drifted away. Sam compares the coming consolidation to 2010s mobile platforms (Android, iOS) where many app categories emerged but only one or two winners survived per category because people have limited cognitive space for tools. He advises builders to keep pace with events because the rate of change is increasing 3-4x, ensure their agents have the capabilities users need, and expect another shakeout wave in the later 2020s.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Welcome to the Harness Era
sections.summary: Sam introduces himself as co-founder/CEO of Mastra, a TypeScript agent framework, and author of 'Principles of Building AI Agents.' He declares the 'harness era' and categorizes harnesses into local, cloud, and open-source framework types. He frames the talk around the agentic spectrum from LLMs to agents to harnesses to claws.

sections.title: Agent vs. LLM and Harness Qualities
sections.summary: Sam distinguishes agents from LLMs via the agent loop, tool calls, memory, retry, context engineering, and agent state. He enumerates harness qualities: durability, doggedness, planning mode, parallel subagents, TUI/slash commands, skills, dynamic agent creation, background bash tasks, autocompact, thread persistence, queue/steer/interrupt, and session-long tool approval.

sections.title: From Local to Cloud (Always-On) Harnesses
sections.summary: Sam describes the ongoing shift from local harnesses to cloud harnesses that are always on, accessible via Slack (including multi-user), mobile apps, and cloud sandboxes. Cloud harnesses enable greater parallelism and push PRs directly to GitHub, but require a different, distributed architecture.

sections.title: Harness-to-Claw Transition: Initiative and Learning
sections.summary: Sam explains the harness-to-claw transition: imbuing harnesses with initiative (external event listening, heartbeat, channels like text/WhatsApp/Telegram, accessible memory, daemon/gateway) and learning (automatic skill generation, code modification). He notes the industry is still exploring the right approaches to continual learning.

sections.title: Steinberger's Law and Predicted Shakeout
sections.summary: Sam coins Steinberger's law: every harness will expand until it becomes a claw, driven by technological, economic, and psychological forces. He draws an analogy to 2010s mobile platforms where many app categories emerged but only one or two winners survived per category due to limited cognitive capacity, predicting a similar shakeout.

sections.title: Shakeout Dynamics and Closing Advice
sections.summary: Sam elaborates the shakeout survival criteria using analogies to Thumbtack, Airbnb, DoorDash, and Uber: a claw must be either economically valuable or frequently used, otherwise it is forgotten like an old college friend. He advises builders to keep pace with events since the rate of change is increasing 3-4x, ensure their agents have the capabilities users need, and expect another shakeout wave in the later 2020s. He closes by reintroducing himself, mentioning his book, and thanking the audience.

limitations: The industry has not yet figured out the right way to do continual learning; options are still being explored.
Sam acknowledges he did not perfectly phrase all the qualities in consistent tense/form.
quantitativeClaims: Mastra has observed agents running in production over the last 18 months.
The shift from local to cloud harnesses has occurred over roughly the last 3 months.
An LLM 18-24 months ago was much simpler than today's harnesses.
The rate of change is increasing 3 to 4x.
Another shakeout wave is expected sometime in the later 2020s.
